=== J27,J25,J4 Opposition Landowners Reply to Exceptions to Proposal for Decision.pdf ===
                                 PUC DOCKET NO. 59475
                               SOAH Docket No. 473-26-16349

JOINT APPLICATION OF ONCOR                    §               BEFORE THE
ELECTRIC DELIVERY COMPANY                     §
LLC AND LCRA TRANSMISSION                     §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
SERVICE CORPORATION TO                        §
AMEND THEIR CERTIFICATES OF                   §                 OF TEXAS
CONVENIENCE AND NECESSITY                     §
FOR THE BELL COUNTY EAST                      §
SWITCH TO BIG HILL SUBSTATION                 §
765-KV TRANSMISSION LINE                      §
PROJECT IN BELL, BURNET, CONCHO,              §
CORYELL, LAMPASAS, LLANO,                     §
MASON, MCCULLOCH, MENARD,                     §
MILAM, MILLS, SAN SABA,                       §
SCHLEICKER, TOM GREEN, AND                    §
WILLLIAMSON COUNTIES


            J27, J25, J4 OPPOSITION LANDOWNERS' REPLY TO
               EXCEPTIONS TO PROPOSAL FOR DECISION


TO THE HONORABLE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:
J27, J25, J4 Opposition Landowners—Bernareggio Family Partners, Ltd., Robert Bowling, and
Wendell “Wendy” & Shirley Fleming (collectively, the “J27 Landowners”)—respectfully submit
this Reply to the Exceptions to the Proposal for Decision (“PFD”). The J27 Landowners rely on
the evidentiary record developed in this proceeding and respond principally to the Exceptions
filed by Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation
(collectively, “Applicants”), Commission Staff (“Staff”), and intervenors advocating approval or
selection of Route 894.


I. INTRODUCTION

The PFD recommends denial because Applicants did not carry their burden to establish
that Import Path 2 is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the
public. Applicants' Exceptions do not cure that failure. Instead, they repeatedly ask the
Commission to treat the PBRP and ERCOT planning recommendations as substitutes for the
project-specific evidence required in this CCN proceeding and to treat “great weight” as if it
were conclusive weight. The record supports neither proposition.

The PFD identified four independent deficiencies: (1) Applicants did not establish the need for
Import Path 2 independently of the broader PBRP; (2) changed load assumptions warranted


                                               1
 reevaluation of the load projections supporting the PBRP recommendation; (3) Applicants did
not establish sufficient generation at Bell County East to perform Import Path 2's asserted
westbound function; and (4) credible evidence showed that new and planned generation in the
Permian Basin could reduce or eliminate the need for the proposed transmission expansion. The
Exceptions do not cure those deficiencies.¹

The J27 Landowners also agree with the many intervenors who oppose Route 894. The post-PFD
Exceptions make clear that the routing question is not simply “487 versus 894.” Several parties
urge the Commission to avoid the Central Corridor altogether because of the State Parks, while
Staff independently recommends Route 487 if the Central Corridor is selected. The
Commission therefore should address the corridor question first, rather than allowing Route
894's performance on two standardized park metrics to decide the broader routing question.²

The August 28, 2026 final order in Docket No. 59315 changes the legal landscape concerning
Rule 22.52(a)(4). The J27 Landowners therefore do not ask the Commission to revisit that
ruling or rely on the public-meeting issue as an independent basis for denial. The factual history
concerning the post-meeting expansion of the routing universe remains relevant, however, when
the Commission evaluates the development of the filed routes and the community-input record.³


II. REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS CONCERNING NEED

A. The PBRP does not eliminate the need for a project-specific showing of need for
Import Path 2.

Applicants' principal argument is that the PBRP, HB 5066, and prior Commission decisions
concerning Import Path 1 effectively establish need for Import Path 2. Applicants characterize
Import Path 2 as an “integrated component” of the PBRP and contend that the PFD's project-
specific analysis improperly unravels the Commission's prior planning decisions.⁴

That argument overstates what the prior proceedings decided. The issue before the Commission
now is whether these Applicants have established that the facilities at issue in this consolidated
proceeding are necessary. The PFD did not reject the PBRP or the importance of ERCOT's
planning work. It asked the more basic question required by a CCN proceeding: whether the
evidence in this record establishes that Import Path 2 remains necessary, can perform its
asserted function, and is supported by the load and generation circumstances actually shown in
the record. The question is not whether the PBRP was reasonable when it was developed; the
question is whether Applicants proved that Import Path 2 remains necessary under the
circumstances shown in this proceeding.

That distinction matters. The PFD expressly found that NERC contingencies and ERCOT's
overarching regional planning are not substitutes for proving project-specific need for
Import Path 2.⁵ The Commission's decisions in Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315 may be relevant
precedent, but they do not establish that every component of the PBRP must be approved
regardless of later-developed evidence. Nor do they relieve Applicants of the burden to establish
the need for this particular Import Path 2 project on this record.


                                                 2
 Indeed, the need question was consolidated in this proceeding precisely so that the Commission
could consider the entirety of Import Path 2. The PFD notes that the western half of Import Path
2 is the Bell County East-to-Big Hill Project and the eastern half is the Big Hill-to-Sand Lake
Project, with the need for the entirety of Import Path 2 determined in this proceeding.⁶

B. “Great weight” to ERCOT does not mean conclusive weight.

Applicants and Staff both argue that the PFD erred by declining to give ERCOT's
recommendation great weight. Applicants further argue that no intervenor performed a
competing power-flow study and therefore the ALJs could not reasonably reach a contrary
conclusion.⁷

The J27 Landowners agree that ERCOT's technical recommendations deserve substantial
consideration. But the rule's “great weight” standard does not transform an ERCOT
planning recommendation into an irrebuttable presumption. The PFD made an alternative
finding that even if ERCOT's recommendation were afforded great weight, the greater weight of
the credible evidence was against the recommendation. That alternative finding is especially
important because it means the Commission can affirm the denial recommendation without
treating the weight question as dispositive.⁸

The record contains more than lay disagreement with ERCOT. It contains ERCOT's own
changed load-forecasting methodology, Commission action recognizing that previously
forecasted loads were coming into service at lower megawatt levels than initially claimed,
evidence of substantial new generation in the Permian Basin, and Applicants' own inability to
identify sufficient source generation or a study establishing that Bell County East can
simultaneously serve Central Texas demand and export the required power westward.⁹ Those are
record facts and evidentiary gaps, not merely competing opinions about electrical engineering.

Nor is a competing full-system power-flow model a prerequisite to finding that an applicant has
not met its burden of proof. Applicants bear the burden of establishing need. If Applicants'
own evidence leaves an essential premise unproven, the Commission need not construct a
substitute engineering study on their behalf. The absence of an intervenor's competing model
therefore does not transform an evidentiary gap in Applicants' case into affirmative proof of
need.

C. The 2025 load-forecasting changes are not being applied “retroactively”; they are
evidence of changed circumstances.

Applicants characterize the PFD's treatment of the 2025 load methodology as an impermissible
retroactive revision of the PBRP. That characterization misses the point. The PFD did not
purport to amend the PBRP. It evaluated whether evidence developed after the PBRP's approval
undermined the assumptions Applicants relied upon to establish present need.

The PFD found that ERCOT's adjusted methodology would materially reduce the non-oil-and-
gas load forecast underlying the PBRP. It specifically found a potential reduction of at least
3,571 MW, compared with an Import Path 2 safe-loading limit of 5,270 MW. The PFD also


                                                3
 found that the PBRP's load forecast had not been retested using the methodology ERCOT
subsequently adopted for its 2025 RTP.¹⁰

Applicants correctly point out that the 2025 methodology was developed for the 2025 RTP rather
than as an express amendment to the PBRP. But that does not answer the evidentiary question.
The fact that ERCOT continued to model the 765-kV paths in the 2025 RTP does not establish
that the underlying PBRP load forecast remains reliable for purposes of this CCN proceeding.
The 2025 RTP itself demonstrates that ERCOT's approach to substantiated load changed because
actual experience showed previously forecasted loads coming into service at lower megawatt
levels than initially claimed.¹¹

Applicants therefore cannot simultaneously argue that the 2025 methodology is sufficiently
relevant to support their own current planning assertions while insisting that the same changed
methodology is irrelevant to the Commission's evaluation of whether the older PBRP
assumptions remain sufficient to prove need.

D. The Far West Texas Import GTCs do not independently prove the need for
Import Path 2.

Applicants' Exceptions place substantial weight on the Far West Texas Import Generic
Transmission Constraints (“GTCs”), arguing that those constraints establish a present-day
reliability need independent of future load growth.¹²

The PFD considered that evidence and rejected the claimed inference. Finding of Fact 112 states
that the Far West Import GTCs had not resulted in load shed to date. Finding of Fact 113
describes the 765-kV import paths as one of seven transmission upgrades ERCOT characterized
as helping to exit the GTCs. Most importantly, Findings of Fact 114 through 116 recognize that
GTCs measure transmission-system constraints but do not validate the composition or reliability
of the load causing the constraint, and that Applicants did not disaggregate the load driving the
GTC from the speculative load undermining the PBRP forecast.¹³

Applicants' Exceptions do not cure that problem. Calling the GTCs a “separate” reliability basis
does not demonstrate that this particular Import Path 2 project is the necessary solution to that
constraint. The PFD's finding is narrower and more persuasive: the GTC evidence does not
establish the durability of the load assumptions supporting the construction of this multibillion-
dollar Import Path 2 project.

The distinction between “help” and “essential” is also significant. The record identified the 765-
kV import paths among the measures that could help address the GTCs. Applicants' Exceptions
elevate that planning description into a finding that all three paths are independently essential.
The Commission should rely on the evidence actually admitted into this record rather than the
stronger characterization advanced in Exceptions.

E. Applicants still have not established that Bell County East can supply the power
Import Path 2 is supposed to deliver westward.



                                                 4
 This is one of the PFD's most concrete findings and one that Applicants' Exceptions do not
adequately answer. The PFD found that Import Path 2 is intended to bring power into the
Permian Basin, not export it; that Applicants did not identify specific generation resources
expected to supply that westward flow; and that Applicants did not prove sufficient power would
be available at Bell County East to transmit westward through Import Path 2.¹⁴

The PFD further found that neither Oncor nor ERCOT studies parsed the Central Texas region's
net generation position under current conditions, projected 2030 conditions, or a 2030 scenario
assuming 50 percent of queued large-load interconnection requests materialize. The PFD found
that Applicants had not determined whether Central Texas generation could serve local data-
center load while simultaneously exporting westward at the line's design capacity.¹⁵

Applicants respond that the broader ERCOT transmission system can provide the required
power. That response does not supply the missing evidence identified by the ALJs. A statewide
interconnected grid may permit power to flow in many directions, but the issue is whether the
asserted function of this particular Import Path 2 segment has been demonstrated under the
conditions Applicants used to justify it. The PFD found that it had not.

This is also why Applicants' criticism of lay witnesses does not resolve the issue. The dispositive
finding is based in significant part on what Applicants did not study or establish. The
Commission does not need to decide that a particular intervenor's engineering theory is correct; it
needs only to determine whether Applicants met their burden with competent evidence. On this
record, the ALJs reasonably found that they did not.

F. The planned and announced Permian Basin gas generation is not required to be a
“committed alternative” before it becomes relevant to the need analysis.

Applicants argue that the PFD improperly treated announced generation as a substitute for
transmission. That is not what the PFD found. The PFD found that circumstances had materially
changed since the PBRP: as of May 13, 2026, 37 planned or announced natural-gas
generation projects in the Permian Basin, West Texas, and Panhandle/Northwest totaled
approximately 39.467 GW, including approximately 25.162 GW among 24 Permian Basin
projects at varying stages of development.¹⁶

Applicants emphasize that only 1.35 GW was under construction as of May 2026. That fact does
not eliminate the evidence's relevance. Applicants bore the burden of proving that the
transmission project was necessary. Once the record showed a dramatically different generation
outlook, Applicants needed to address whether that changed generation picture altered the need
for long-distance imports. The PFD found that they did not adequately do so.

The point is not that all 39 GW will necessarily be built, or that every announced project will be
available on a particular date. The point is that the factual premise underlying the original
planning analysis has materially changed, and Applicants did not demonstrate that the
changed generation outlook leaves Import Path 2 necessary. That changed picture therefore
creates an evidentiary question Applicants were required to address before the Commission
could find that a multibillion-dollar import path remains necessary.


                                                 5
 Nothing in the PFD's denial recommendation requires the Commission to conclude that no
transmission improvements are needed in the Permian Basin. The issue is whether
Applicants proved the necessity of this particular Import Path 2 project. A finding that Import
Path 2 has not been proven necessary is not a finding that local transmission improvements or
other reliability measures are unnecessary.

Applicants also argue that generation cannot substitute for transmission because generation is
market-driven and its location and timing are uncertain. But that argument cuts both ways. If
generation location, timing, and deliverability are uncertain, then the same uncertainty makes it
difficult to establish that a particular long-distance transmission path is presently necessary based
on an older forecast that assumed a materially different generation picture.

G. Prior Import Path 1 decisions do not require approval of Import Path 2 on this
record.

Applicants and Delaware Basin Midstream rely heavily on the Commission's August 28, 2026
decisions in Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315. Those decisions are relevant, but they do not make
the present proceeding a ministerial extension of those cases. The PFD in this docket addressed
evidence specifically developed concerning Import Path 2, including the Bell County East
injection point, the Central Texas generation position, and the changed Permian Basin generation
outlook.¹⁷

Nor should the Commission treat a difference between this PFD and the companion decisions as
an impermissible conflict in Commission policy. A contested case is decided on its own
evidentiary record. If the record in this proceeding establishes additional deficiencies, the
Commission is not required to disregard them merely to make the outcome identical to another
docket.

The strongest reading of the companion orders is therefore not that they foreclose denial here,
but that they provide precedent concerning the weight of the PBRP and ERCOT
recommendations. The Commission can give those recommendations substantial weight and still
conclude that the evidence specific to Import Path 2 is insufficient.


III. REPLY TO ROUTING EXCEPTIONS
A. The emerging consensus in the Exceptions confirms that Route 894 does not
eliminate the Central Corridor's State Park problem.

A significant portion of the post-PFD Exceptions now agrees with the J27 Landowners' basic
routing concern. Staten Creek Ranch urges the Commission to reject Route 894 because the
Central Corridor would severely affect Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park,
and instead favors a Northern Corridor route such as Route 392 or Route 410, with Route 296 as
an alternative.¹⁸ Other intervenors likewise point to Routes 296, 392, 410, or Cherokee Creek G
as alternatives that reduce the State Park impacts.



                                                 6
 This matters because the debate should not be framed as “Route 894 versus Route 487.” The
record contains multiple corridors. The PFD itself found that Route 894 would remain visible
from many areas of both parks and that its Link J22 crossing is close to the protected and
recreational lands associated with the parks.¹⁹

The J27 Landowners therefore respectfully disagree with Staff's suggestion that the park factor
should cease to distinguish routes merely because Routes 487 and 894 both have some impact.
Staff's point may be useful at the second step—choosing between 487 and 894—but it does not
answer the first step. The Commission must still decide whether a Central Corridor route is the
best overall accommodation when reasonable alternatives place the line farther from the two
State Parks. A route can be preferable to another route within the Central Corridor and still be
inferior to a reasonable route outside that corridor.

B. Route 894's “zero” park metric is a measurement result, not a finding of zero
visual impact.

Applicants and several intervenors supporting Route 894 emphasize its best-possible numerical
performance on the standardized park measures: no park or recreational area within 1,000 feet
of the centerline and zero miles of right-of-way within the defined one-half-mile foreground
visual zone. The J27 Landowners concede that these are numerical advantages.²⁰

But the record does not support treating those two measures as two independent, dispositive
reasons to select Route 894. They are overlapping measurements of proximity to the same
underlying park resource. More importantly, the PFD expressly recognized that the
Environmental Assessment's statistical information does not completely capture park impacts.
The record also contains TPWD viewshed analysis stating that a 150- to 200-foot transmission
line and tower within five miles of a scenic viewpoint valued for natural qualities is likely to be
distracting to most visitors, and TPWD recommended a buffer of at least five miles from
important scenic points.²¹

Route 894's Link J22 is particularly important. It crosses the Colorado River close to the parks
and continues through a landscape from which the line will be visible. The fact that J22 falls
outside the one-half-mile foreground visual-zone statistic does not transform the viewshed into a
non-impact. The evidence describes the visual environment in terms of overlooks, trails, park
headquarters, the Colorado River valley, and Post Oak Falls—not merely in terms of a half-mile
GIS threshold.

The J27 Landowners therefore do not ask the Commission to disregard the standardized metric.
We ask the Commission to give it the weight the record supports: significant, but not dispositive.

TPWD's concerns are particularly important because the attributes for which Post Oak Ridge
State Park is being protected include “scenic destinations and overlook opportunities.” The
visual relationship between a transmission line and the park therefore goes directly to the scenic
and recreational qualities TPWD has identified for the park. The J27 Landowners' own route-
segment mapping provides an additional illustration of why the choice of park metric matters.
Looking beyond the Environmental Assessment's one-half-mile foreground-zone measure, our


                                                 7
 mapping of Route 487's J11 segment and Route 894's J22-J23-J27 segments indicates that Route
894 has greater exposure within the five-mile area that TPWD recommended protecting
around the parks' most scenic points. It also indicates greater exposure at the closer end of that
viewshed: approximately 6.24 miles of Route 894 are within 1.25 miles of the parks,
compared with approximately 4.52 miles for Route 487. These are estimates, not official
routing metrics, and are not offered as a substitute for the EA analysis. They illustrate a narrower
point: Route 894's advantage under the one-half-mile metric should not be treated as
synonymous with lesser real-world viewshed impact.

C. The State Park issue should be resolved at the corridor level before the
Commission compares 487 and 894.

The Commission has previously made routing tradeoffs to protect significant park and scenic
resources. The record cited in the Exceptions includes Docket No. 38290, where the Commission
selected a route that was longer, more expensive, and more impactful to habitable structures in
order to avoid the Palo Duro Canyon area, even though the line did not directly encroach on the
State Park. The record also includes Docket No. 37448, where the proposed transmission line
was routed away from Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Falls.²²

The J27 Landowners do not contend that these cases establish a mandatory rule that parks always
trump cost, length, or other factors. They establish something narrower and more useful: the
Commission may give substantial qualitative weight to a unique scenic or recreational resource
when the quantitative differences among routes are relatively modest.

The Commission's August 28, 2026 decision in Docket No. 59315 provides a particularly useful
example of that balancing. In that proceeding, the Commission adopted Route 559, which
avoided Dinosaur Valley State Park, even though Route 559 was approximately $27 million
more expensive than Route 552 and affected the same number of habitable structures. The PFD
nevertheless identified park avoidance, together with strong paralleling and other routing
characteristics, as reasons supporting Route 559. The precedent does not make park avoidance
dispositive; it demonstrates that meaningful park protection may justify reasonable tradeoffs
in other routing factors when the overall balance supports it.

Here, Route 296 is approximately 3.82 miles from Colorado Bend State Park and 3.22 miles
from Post Oak Ridge State Park, while Routes 392 and 410 are approximately 9.39 and 9.83
miles from the two parks. Route CCG is also a record-supported Southern Corridor alternative.²³
These routes demonstrate that the Commission is not forced to accept a new 765-kV corridor
within roughly a mile of these State Parks with the alternatives available to it.

D. Route 487 should be selected if the Commission nevertheless chooses the Central
Corridor.

The J27 Landowners agree with Staff on this point. Staff independently recommends Route
487 and continues to describe it as the route that best meets the governing criteria.²⁴ That
recommendation is particularly persuasive because it comes from the Commission's own



                                                 8
 technical staff and reflects an evaluation of the full route universe rather than a single intervenor
preference.

Route 487's strongest distinction is its use of existing compatible infrastructure. The routing data
show approximately 109.95 miles of compatible-ROW paralleling for Route 487, or 49.64
percent of the route, versus 98.02 miles, or 43.92 percent, for Route 894. Route 487 also
parallels approximately 22.05 miles of existing electric transmission lines, compared with only
5.66 miles for Route 894—nearly four times as much.²⁵

That difference is not merely aesthetic. Existing-corridor paralleling can reduce the creation of
additional standalone transmission corridors and therefore can moderate fragmentation and the
distribution of impacts among landowners. Staff specifically emphasized the distinction between
the routes' compatible-ROW performance and concluded that Route 487's total length and
paralleling characteristics favored its selection.²⁶

Route 487 also has a modest advantage in route length and transmission-line cost. The
Applicants' Combined Data Table estimates approximately $1.665 billion for Route 487 versus
$1.681 billion for Route 894, a difference of approximately $16.1 million. Route 487 is also
approximately 1.7 miles shorter. These differences are not independently dispositive, but they
point in the same direction as the substantial paralleling advantage.²⁷

E. Route 894's habitable-structure advantage is narrower than the headline count
suggests.

The J27 Landowners do not dispute that Route 894 performs slightly better under the broad
habitable-structure measure: 85 versus 96 structures within 500 feet of the centerline. That is an
important prudent-avoidance consideration.

The underlying structure categories, however, show that the difference is not 11 additional
single-family homes. The record identifies 80 single-family residences for Route 894 and 85
for Route 487—a difference of five. The broader 11-structure difference includes other
structure categories, including mobile living units.²⁸

This distinction does not mean those other structures are unimportant. It means the Commission
should weigh the prudent-avoidance difference accurately against the other routing criteria rather
than allowing the broad count to obscure the comparative record.

Staff's system-wide analysis also supports Route 487. Staff found that Route 487 ranked 23rd
among 132 alternatives in habitable-structure performance and that most of the routes
performing better on that measure carried substantial tradeoffs in cost, length, or compatible-
ROW paralleling.²⁹ The prudent-avoidance criterion was therefore considered in Staff's overall
balancing; it did not stand alone.

F. The remaining quantitative record does not establish Route 894's overall
superiority.



                                                  9
 The post-PFD Exceptions identify several areas in which Route 894 performs better than Route
487, including riparian mileage, wetlands, lakes, rare plants, recorded cultural resources,
heliports, electronic/communications constraints, and certain road and highway metrics. The J27
Landowners do not dispute those disadvantages to Route 487.
But the Commission's task is not to identify the route that wins the largest number of isolated
spreadsheet cells. It is to balance the statutory criteria. Route 487 has 282 mapped stream
crossings versus 291 for Route 894; 0.07 miles of known federally listed species habitat
versus 0.09; and approximately 266.934 miles of high archaeological/historical-potential area
versus 278.115 miles.³⁰ It also has fewer nearby private airstrips and fewer applicable FAA-
registered airport constraints in the measures identified in the routing data.

The cumulative record therefore does not support the proposition that Route 894 is affirmatively
superior. It supports a close balancing judgment of Route 894 and 487’s park-proximity
problems, comparable habitable-structure performance and Route 487's substantial compatible-
infrastructure paralleling, lower cost, shorter length, and other cumulative advantages.

G. The PFD's “least bad option” characterization should not be converted into a
presumption favoring Route 894.

The PFD stated that the ALJs were “tasked with choosing the least bad option” and
recommended Route 894 “if any route must be chosen.”³¹ The J27 Landowners do not contend
that this wording constitutes legal error. But it is relevant to the weight the Commission should
give the recommendation.

A recommendation framed as the “least bad option” is not the same as a finding that Route
894 affirmatively best satisfies the statutory criteria. The Commission remains responsible for
independently balancing the record. That is particularly important where Staff independently
reached the opposite conclusion and recommended Route 487.

The Commission should therefore ask two straightforward questions. First, is the Central
Corridor justified when other reasonable corridors would reduce the line's proximity to the State
Parks? Second, if the Central Corridor is selected, do Route 894's park-proximity issues and
similar habitable structures outweigh Route 487's materially greater use of existing compatible
infrastructure, nearly four times the existing transmission-line paralleling, shorter length, lower
estimated transmission-line cost, favorable secondary metrics, and Staff's independent
recommendation? On this record, the J27 Landowners submit that the answer to both questions is
no.


IV. LIMITED REPLY REGARDING NOTICE AND PUBLIC INPUT

The J27 Landowners do not rely on the PFD's notice conclusions as an independent basis for
denial. The Commission's August 28, 2026 order in Docket No. 59315 held that Rule
22.52(a)(4) requires at least one public meeting before filing but does not require an additional
meeting merely because route links are later added or the study area is expanded.³³



                                                10
 Applicants nevertheless use that decision to argue, in substance, that the post-meeting route
changes should have no significance beyond establishing compliance with the rule. The J27
Landowners respectfully disagree with that broader proposition. Compliance with Rule
22.52(a)(4) does not mean that the history of the route-development process becomes irrelevant
to the Commission's evaluation of community values, route development, or the weight to be
assigned to later-added corridors.

The PFD found that approximately 400 miles of route links were added after the June 2025
public meetings, bringing approximately 1,400 additional landowners into the filed routing
universe.³⁴ Those facts may not establish a notice violation after Docket No. 59315, but they
remain relevant to understanding which portions of the final routing universe were available for
landowner input at the public meetings and which were developed later.

That distinction is particularly relevant to the Commission's understanding of the final routing
universe. The record shows that substantial portions of the filed routing universe were added or
modified after the public meetings. The Commission need not treat those changes as a notice
violation to recognize the route-development history as factual context when evaluating
community values, the development of alternatives, and the relative merits of the final routes.


V. REQUESTED DISPOSITION

The J27 Landowners respectfully request that the Commission reject the Exceptions that seek to
overturn the PFD's recommendation of denial and adopt the PFD's conclusion that Applicants
failed to establish the need for Import Path 2.

If the Commission nevertheless determines that the Project should proceed, the J27 Landowners
request that the Commission first consider whether a route outside the Central Corridor
provides a better overall balance of the statutory criteria and better protects Colorado Bend State
Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park. Route CCG is one record-supported example; Routes 296,
392, and 410 are additional examples raised in the Exceptions and record.

If the Commission nevertheless selects the Central Corridor, the J27 Landowners request
selection of Route 487 rather than Route 894. Route 894’s mixed performance on park proximity
and similar habitable-structure count are minor advantages. They do not eliminate the Central
Corridor's broader park and viewshed impacts and do not outweigh Route 487's materially
greater use of existing compatible infrastructure, nearly four times the existing transmission-
line paralleling, shorter length, lower estimated transmission-line cost, favorable secondary
metrics, and Staff's independent recommendation.


VI. PROPOSED FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS

The J27 Landowners do not request a wholesale rewrite of the PFD. If the Commission adopts
the PFD's denial recommendation, the existing need findings and conclusions should be retained,




                                                11
 subject to the Commission's August 28, 2026 ruling in Docket No. 59315 concerning Rule
22.52(a)(4).

If the Commission reaches routing, the final order should expressly identify the relative weight
assigned to: (1) the State Park and viewshed evidence; (2) Route 487's 49.64 percent compatible-
ROW paralleling compared with Route 894's 43.92 percent; (3) Route 487's 22.05 miles of
existing transmission-line paralleling compared with 5.66 miles; (4) the $16.1 million
transmission-line cost difference and 1.7-mile length difference; (5) the 96-versus-85 broad
habitable-structure comparison and the narrower 85-versus-80 single-family comparison; and (6)
Staff's independent recommendation of Route 487.³⁶


VII. CONCLUSION

For the reasons stated above, the J27 Landowners respectfully request that the Commission deny
the Applications because Applicants failed to establish that Import Path 2 is necessary for the
service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public.

Alternatively, if the Commission approves the Project, it should first consider a non-Central-
Corridor alternative that better protects Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State
Park. If the Commission nevertheless selects the Central Corridor, it should select Route 487
rather than Route 894.

Respectfully submitted,

J27, J25, J4 OPPOSITION LANDOWNERS

Bernareggio Family Partners, Ltd.
Robert Bowling
Wendell “Wendy” & Shirley Fleming

By: /s/ Paul Grimme
Paul Grimme, Representative
J27, J25, J4 Opposition Landowners



CERTIFICATE OF SERVICE

I certify that a true and correct copy of the foregoing instrument has been served on all parties of
record on this 9th day of September 2026.

/s/ Paul Grimme
Paul Grimme

I. INTRODUCTION

The PFD recommends denial because Applicants did not carry their burden to establish
that Import Path 2 is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the
public. Applicants' Exceptions do not cure that failure. Instead, they repeatedly ask the
Commission to treat the PBRP and ERCOT planning recommendations as substitutes for the
project-specific evidence required in this CCN proceeding and to treat "great weight" as if it
were conclusive weight. The record supports neither proposition.

The PFD identified four independent deficiencies: (1) Applicants did not establish the need for
Import Path 2 independently of the broader PBRP; (2) changed load assumptions warranted


                                                 1
 reevaluation of the load projections supporting the PBRP recommendation; (3) Applicants did
not establish sufficient generation at Bell County East to perform Import Path 2's asserted
westbound function; and (4) credible evidence showed that new and planned generation in the
Permian Basin could reduce or eliminate the need for the proposed transmission expansion. The
Exceptions do not cure those deficiencies.1

The J27 Landowners also agree with the many intervenors who oppose Route 894. The post-PFD
Exceptions make clear that the routing question is not simply "487 versus 894." Several parties
urge the Commission to avoid the Central Corridor altogether because of the State Parks, while
Staff independently recommends Route 487 if the Central Corridor is selected. The
Commission therefore should address the corridor question first, rather than allowing Route
894's performance on two standardized park metrics to decide the broader routing question.2

The August 28,2026 final order in Docket No. 59315 changes the legal landscape concerning
Rule 22.52(a)(4). The J27 Landowners therefore do not ask the Commission to revisit that
ruling or rely on the public-meeting issue as an independent basis for denial. The factual history
concerning the post-meeting expansion of the routing universe remains relevant, however, when
the Commission evaluates the development of the filed routes and the community-input record.3


II. REPLY TO EXCEPTIONS CONCERNING NEED

A. The PBRP does not eliminate the need for a project-specific showing of need for
Import Path 2.

Applicants' principal argument is that the PBRP, HB 5066, and prior Commission decisions
concerning Import Path 1 effectively establish need for Import Path 2. Applicants characterize
Import Path 2 as an "integrated componenf' of the PBRP and contend that the PFD's project-
specific analysis improperly unravels the Commission's prior planning decisions.4

That argument overstates what the prior proceedings decided. The issue before the Commission
now is whether these Applicants have established that the facilities at issue in this consolidated
proceeding are necessary. The PFD did not reject the PBRP or the importance of ERCOT's
planning work. It asked the more basic question required by a CCN proceeding: whether the
evidence in this record establishes that Import Path 2 remains necessary, can perform its
asserted function, and is supported by the load and generation circumstances actually shown in
the record. The question is not whether the PBRP was reasonable when it was developed; the
question is whether Applicants proved that Import Path 2 remains necessary under the
circumstances shown in this proceeding.

That distinction matters. The PFD expressly found that NERC contingencies and ERCOT's
overarching regional planning are not substitutes for proving project-specific need for
Import Path 2.5 The Commission's decisions in Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315 may be relevant
precedent, but they do not establish that every component of the PBRP must be approved
regardless of later-developed evidence. Nor do they relieve Applicants of the burden to establish
the need for this particular Import Path 2 project on this record.



                                                 2
 Indeed, the need question was consolidated in this proceeding precisely so that the Commission
could consider the entirety of Import Path 2. The PFD notes that the western half of Import Path
2 is the Bell County East-to-Big Hill Project and the eastern half is the Big Hill-to-Sand Lake
Project, with the need for the entirety of Import Path 2 determined in this proceeding.6

B. "Great weight" to ERCOT does not mean conclusive weight.

Applicants and Staff both argue that the PFD erred by declining to give ERCOT's
recommendation great weight. Applicants further argue that no intervenor performed a
competing power-flow study and therefore the ALJs could not reasonably reach a contrary
conclusion.7

The J27 Landowners agree that ERCOT's technical recommendations deserve substantial
consideration. But the rule's "great weight" standard does not transform an ERCOT
planning recommendation into an irrebuttable presumption. The PFD made an alternative
finding that even if ERCOT's recommendation were afforded great weight, the greater weight of
the credible evidence was against the recommendation. That alternative finding is especially
important because it means the Commission can affirm the denial recommendation without
treating the weight question as dispositive.8

The record contains more than lay disagreement with ERCOT. It contains ERCOT's own
changed load-forecasting methodology, Commission action recognizing that previously
forecasted loads were coming into service at lower megawatt levels than initially claimed,
evidence of substantial new generation in the Permian Basin, and Applicants' own inability to
identify sufficient source generation or a study establishing that Bell County East can
simultaneously serve Central Texas demand and export the required power westward.9 Those are
record facts and evidentiary gaps, not merely competing opinions about electrical engineering.

Nor is a competing full-system power-flow model a prerequisite to finding that an applicant has
not met its burden of proof. Applicants bear the burden of establishing need. If Applicants'
own evidence leaves an essential premise unproven, the Commission need not construct a
substitute engineering study on their behalf. The absence of an intervenor's competing model
therefore does not transform an evidentiary gap in Applicants' case into affirmative proof of
need.
C. The 2025 load-forecasting changes are not being applied "retroactively"; they are
evidence of changed circumstances.

Applicants characterize the PFD's treatment of the 2025 load methodology as an impermissible
retroactive revision of the PBRP. That characterization misses the point. The PFD did not
purport to amend the PBRP. It evaluated whether evidence developed after the PBRP's approval
undermined the assumptions Applicants relied upon to establish present need.

The PFD found that ERCOT's adjusted methodology would materially reduce the non-oil-and-
gas load forecast underlying the PBRP. It specifically found a potential reduction of at least
3,571 MW, compared with an Import Path 2 safe-loading limit of 5,270 MW. The PFD also



                                                3
 found that the PBRP's load forecast had not been retested using the methodology ERCOT
subsequently adopted for its 2025 RTP.10

Applicants correctly point out that the 2025 methodology was developed for the 2025 RTP rather
than as an express amendment to the PBRP. But that does not answer the evidentiary question.
The fact that ERCOT continued to model the 765-kV paths in the 2025 RTP does not establish
that the underlying PBRP load forecast remains reliable for purposes of this CCN proceeding.
The 2025 RTP itself demonstrates that ERCOT's approach to substantiated load changed because
actual experience showed previously forecasted loads coming into service at lower megawatt
levels than initially claimed.11

Applicants therefore cannot simultaneously argue that the 2025 methodology is sufficiently
relevant to support their own current planning assertions while insisting that the same changed
methodology is irrelevant to the Commission's evaluation of whether the older PBRP
assumptions remain sufficient to prove need.

D. The Far West Texas Import GTCs do not independently prove the need for
Import Path 2.

Applicants' Exceptions place substantial weight on the Far West Texas Import Generic
Transmission Constraints ("GTCs"), arguing that those constraints establish a present-day
reliability need independent of future load growth.12

The PFD considered that evidence and rej ected the claimed inference. Finding of Fact 112 states
that the Far West Import GTCs had not resulted in load shed to date. Finding of Fact 113
describes the 765-kV import paths as one of seven transmission upgrades ERCOT characterized
as helping to exit the GTCs. Most importantly, Findings of Fact 114 through 116 recognize that
GTCs measure transmission-system constraints but do not validate the composition or reliability
of the load causing the constraint, and that Applicants did not disaggregate the load driving the
GTC from the speculative load undermining the PBRP forecast. 13

Applicants' Exceptions do not cure that problem. Calling the GTCs a "separate" reliability basis
does not demonstrate that this particular Import Path 2 proj ect is the necessary solution to that
constraint. The PFD's finding is narrower and more persuasive: the GTC evidence does not
establish the durability of the load assumptions supporting the construction of this multibillion-
dollar Import Path 2 proj ect.

The distinction between "help" and "essential" is also significant. The record identified the 765-
kV import paths among the measures that could help address the GTCs. Applicants' Exceptions
elevate that planning description into a finding that all three paths are independently essential.
The Commission should rely on the evidence actually admitted into this record rather than the
stronger characterization advanced in Exceptions.

E. Applicants still have not established that Bell County East can supply the power
Import Path 2 is supposed to deliver westward.




                                                 4
 This is one of the PFD's most concrete findings and one that Applicants' Exceptions do not
adequately answer. The PFD found that Import Path 2 is intended to bring power into the
Permian Basin, not export it; that Applicants did not identify specific generation resources
expected to supply that westward flow; and that Applicants did not prove sufficient power would
be available at Bell County East to transmit westward through Import Path 2.14

The PFD further found that neither Oncor nor ERCOT studies parsed the Central Texas region's
net generation position under current conditions, projected 2030 conditions, or a 2030 scenario
assuming 50 percent of queued large-load interconnection requests materialize. The PFD found
that Applicants had not determined whether Central Texas generation could serve local data-
center load while simultaneously exporting westward at the line's design capacity.15

Applicants respond that the broader ERCOT transmission system can provide the required
power. That response does not supply the missing evidence identified by the ALJs. A statewide
interconnected grid may permit power to flow in many directions, but the issue is whether the
asserted function of this particular Import Path 2 segment has been demonstrated under the
conditions Applicants used to justify it. The PFD found that it had not.

This is also why Applicants' criticism of lay witnesses does not resolve the issue. The dispositive
finding is based in significant part on what Applicants did not study or establish. The
Commission does not need to decide that a particular intervenor's engineering theory is correct; it
needs only to determine whether Applicants met their burden with competent evidence. On this
record, the ALJs reasonably found that they did not.

F. The planned and announced Permian Basin gas generation is not required to be a
"committed alternative" before it becomes relevant to the need analysis.

Applicants argue that the PFD improperly treated announced generation as a substitute for
transmission. That is not what the PFD found. The PFD found that circumstances had materially
changed since the PBRP: as of May 13, 2026, 37 planned or announced natural-gas
generation projects in the Permian Basin, West Texas, and Panhandle/Northwest totaled
approximately 39.467 GW, including approximately 25.162 GW among 24 Permian Basin
proj ects at varying stages of development. 16

Applicants emphasize that only 1.35 GW was under construction as of May 2026. That fact does
not eliminate the evidence's relevance. Applicants bore the burden of proving that the
transmission project was necessary. Once the record showed a dramatically different generation
outlook, Applicants needed to address whether that changed generation picture altered the need
for long-distance imports. The PFD found that they did not adequately do so.

The point is not that all 39 GW will necessarily be built, or that every announced project will be
available on a particular date. The point is that the factual premise underlying the original
planning analysis has materially changed, and Applicants did not demonstrate that the
changed generation outlook leaves Import Path 2 necessary. That changed picture therefore
creates an evidentiary question Applicants were required to address before the Commission
could find that a multibillion-dollar import path remains necessary.


                                                 5
 Nothing in the PFD's denial recommendation requires the Commission to conclude that no
transmission improvements are needed in the Permian Basin. The issue is whether
Applicants proved the necessity of this particular Import Path 2 project. A finding that Import
Path 2 has not been proven necessary is not a finding that local transmission improvements or
other reliability measures are unnecessary.

Applicants also argue that generation cannot substitute for transmission because generation is
market-driven and its location and timing are uncertain. But that argument cuts both ways. If
generation location, timing, and deliverability are uncertain, then the same uncertainty makes it
difficult to establish that a particular long-distance transmission path is presently necessary based
on an older forecast that assumed a materially different generation picture.

G. Prior Import Path 1 decisions do not require approval of Import Path 2 on this
record.

Applicants and Delaware Basin Midstream rely heavily on the Commission's August 28,2026
decisions in Docket Nos. 59029 and 59315. Those decisions are relevant, but they do not make
the present proceeding a ministerial extension of those cases. The PFD in this docket addressed
evidence specifically developed concerning Import Path 2, including the Bell County East
inj ection point, the Central Texas generation position, and the changed Permian Basin generation
outlook. 17

Nor should the Commission treat a difference between this PFD and the companion decisions as
an impermissible conflict in Commission policy. A contested case is decided on its own
evidentiary record. If the record in this proceeding establishes additional deficiencies, the
Commission is not required to disregard them merely to make the outcome identical to another
docket
The strongest reading of the companion orders is therefore not that they foreclose denial here,
but that they provide precedent concerning the weight of the PBRP and ERCOT
recommendations. The Commission can give those recommendations substantial weight and still
conclude that the evidence specific to Import Path 2 is insufficient.


III. REPLY TO ROUTING EXCEPTIONS

A. The emerging consensus in the Exceptions confirms that Route 894 does not
eliminate the Central Corridor's State Park problem.

A significant portion of the post-PFD Exceptions now agrees with the J27 Landowners' basic
routing concern. Staten Creek Ranch urges the Commission to reject Route 894 because the
Central Corridor would severely affect Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park,
and instead favors a Northern Corridor route such as Route 392 or Route 410, with Route 296 as
an alternative.18 Other intervenors likewise point to Routes 296, 392, 410, or Cherokee Creek G
as alternatives that reduce the State Park impacts.




                                                  6
 This matters because the debate should not be framed as "Route 894 versus Route 487." The
record contains multiple corridors. The PFD itself found that Route 894 would remain visible
from many areas of both parks and that its Link J22 crossing is close to the protected and
recreational lands associated with the parks. 19

The J27 Landowners therefore respectfully disagree with Staff's suggestion that the park factor
should cease to distinguish routes merely because Routes 487 and 894 both have some impact.
Staff's point may be useful at the second step--choosing between 487 and 894-but it does not
answer the first step. The Commission must still decide whether a Central Corridor route is the
best overall accommodation when reasonable alternatives place the line farther from the two
State Parks. A route can be preferable to another route within the Central Corridor and still be
inferior to a reasonable route outside that corridor.

B. Route 894's " zero " park metric is a measurement result, not a finding of zero
visual impact.

Applicants and several intervenors supporting Route 894 emphasize its best-possible numerical
performance on the standardized park measures: no park or recreational area within 1,000 feet
of the centerline and zero miles of right-of-way within the defined one-half-mile foreground
visual zone. The J27 Landowners concede that these are numerical advantages.20

But the record does not support treating those two measures as two independent, dispositive
reasons to select Route 894. They are overlapping measurements of proximity to the same
underlying park resource. More importantly, the PFD expressly recognized that the
Environmental Assessment's statistical information does not completely capture park impacts.
The record also contains TPWD viewshed analysis stating that a 150- to 200-foot transmission
line and tower within five miles of a scenic viewpoint valued for natural qualities is likely to be
distracting to most visitors, and TPWD recommended a buffer of at least five miles from
important scenic points.21

Route 894's Link J22 is particularly important. It crosses the Colorado River close to the parks
and continues through a landscape from which the line will be visible. The fact that J22 falls
outside the one-half-mile foreground visual-zone statistic does not transform the viewshed into a
non-impact. The evidence describes the visual environment in terms of overlooks, trails, park
headquarters, the Colorado River valley, and Post Oak Falls-not merely in terms of a half-mile
GIS threshold.

The J27 Landowners therefore do not ask the Commission to disregard the standardized metric.
We ask the Commission to give it the weight the record supports: significant, but not dispositive.

TPWD's concerns are particularly important because the attributes for which Post Oak Ridge
State Park is being protected include "scenic destinations and overlook opportunities." The
visual relationship between a transmission line and the park therefore goes directly to the scenic
and recreational qualities TPWD has identified for the park. The J27 Landowners' own route-
segment mapping provides an additional illustration of why the choice of park metric matters.
Looking beyond the Environmental Assessment's one-half-mile foreground-zone measure, our



                                                   7
 mapping of Route 487's Jll segment and Route 894's J22-J23-J27 segments indicates that Route
894 has greater exposure within the five-mile area that TPWD recommended protecting
around the parks' most scenic points. It also indicates greater exposure at the closer end of that
viewshed: approximately 6.24 miles of Route 894 are within 1.25 miles of the parks,
compared with approximately 4.52 miles for Route 487. These are estimates, not official
routing metrics, and are not offered as a substitute for the EA analysis. They illustrate a narrower
point: Route 894's advantage under the one-half-mile metric should not be treated as
synonymous with lesser real-world viewshed impact.

C. The State Park issue should be resolved at the corridor level before the
Commission compares 487 and 894.

The Commission has previously made routing tradeoffs to protect significant park and scenic
resources. The record cited in the Exceptions includes Docket No. 38290, where the Commission
selected a route that was longer, more expensive, and more impactful to habitable structures in
order to avoid the Palo Duro Canyon area, even though the line did not directly encroach on the
State Park. The record also includes Docket No. 37448, where the proposed transmission line
was routed away from Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Falls.22

The J27 Landowners do not contend that these cases establish a mandatory rule that parks always
trump cost, length, or other factors. They establish something narrower and more useful: the
Commission may give substantial qualitative weight to a unique scenic or recreational resource
when the quantitative differences among routes are relatively modest.

The Commission's August 28,2026 decision in Docket No. 59315 provides a particularly useful
example of that balancing. In that proceeding, the Commission adopted Route 559, which
avoided Dinosaur Valley State Park, even though Route 559 was approximately $27 million
more expensive than Route 552 and affected the same number of habitable structures. The PFD
nevertheless identified park avoidance, together with strong paralleling and other routing
characteristics, as reasons supporting Route 559. The precedent does not make park avoidance
dispositive; it demonstrates that meaningful park protection may justify reasonable tradeoffs
in other routing factors when the overall balance supports it.

Here, Route 296 is approximately 3.82 miles from Colorado Bend State Park and 3.22 miles
from Post Oak Ridge State Park, while Routes 392 and 410 are approximately 9.39 and 9.83
miles from the two parks. Route CCG is also a record-supported Southern Corridor alternative.23
These routes demonstrate that the Commission is not forced to accept a new 765-kV corridor
within roughly a mile of these State Parks with the alternatives available to it.

D. Route 487 should be selected if the Commission nevertheless chooses the Central
Corridor.

The J27 Landowners agree with Staff on this point. Staff independently recommends Route
487 and continues to describe it as the route that best meets the governing criteria.24 That
recommendation is particularly persuasive because it comes from the Commission's own



                                                 8
 technical staff and reflects an evaluation of the full route universe rather than a single intervenor
preference.

Route 487's strongest distinction is its use of existing compatible infrastructure. The routing data
show approximately 109.95 miles of compatible-ROW paralleling for Route 487, or 49.64
percent of the route, versus 98.02 miles, or 43.92 percent, for Route 894. Route 487 also
parallels approximately 22.05 miles of existing electric transmission lines, compared with only
5.66 miles for Route 894-nearly four times as much.25

That difference is not merely aesthetic. Existing-corridor paralleling can reduce the creation of
additional standalone transmission corridors and therefore can moderate fragmentation and the
distribution of impacts among landowners. Staff specifically emphasized the distinction between
the routes' compatible-ROW performance and concluded that Route 487's total length and
paralleling characteristics favored its selection.26

Route 487 also has a modest advantage in route length and transmission-line cost. The
Applicants' Combined Data Table estimates approximately $1.665 billion for Route 487 versus
$1.681 billion for Route 894, a difference of approximately $16.1 million. Route 487 is also
approximately 1.7 miles shorter. These differences are not independently dispositive, but they
point in the same direction as the substantial paralleling advantage.27

E. Route 894's habitable-structure advantage is narrower than the headline count
suggests.

The J27 Landowners do not dispute that Route 894 performs slightly better under the broad
habitable-structure measure: 85 versus 96 structures within 500 feet of the centerline. That is an
important prudent-avoidance consideration.

The underlying structure categories, however, show that the difference is not 11 additional
single-family homes. The record identifies 80 single-family residences for Route 894 and 85
for Route 487-a difference of five. The broader 11-structure difference includes other
structure categories, including mobile living units.28

This distinction does not mean those other structures are unimportant. It means the Commission
should weigh the prudent-avoidance difference accurately against the other routing criteria rather
than allowing the broad count to obscure the comparative record.

Staff's system-wide analysis also supports Route 487. Staff found that Route 487 ranked 23rd
among 132 alternatives in habitable-structure performance and that most of the routes
performing better on that measure carried substantial tradeoffs in cost, length, or compatible-
ROW paralleling.29 The prudent-avoidance criterion was therefore considered in Staff's overall
balancing; it did not stand alone.

F. The remaining quantitative record does not establish Route 894's overall
superiority.



                                                  9
 The post-PFD Exceptions identify several areas in which Route 894 performs better than Route
487, including riparian mileage, wetlands, lakes, rare plants, recorded cultural resources,
heliports, electronic/communications constraints, and certain road and highway metrics. The J27
Landowners do not dispute those disadvantages to Route 487.
But the Commission's task is not to identify the route that wins the largest number of isolated
spreadsheet cells. It is to balance the statutory criteria. Route 487 has 282 mapped stream
cross ings versus 291 for Route 894; 0.07 miles of known federally listed species habitat
versus 0.09; and approximately 266.934 miles of high archaeological/historical-potential area
versus 278.115 miles.3° It also has fewer nearby private airstrips and fewer applicable FAA-
registered airport constraints in the measures identified in the routing data.

The cumulative record therefore does not support the proposition that Route 894 is affirmatively
superior. It supports a close balancing judgment of Route 894 and 487's park-proximity
problems, comparable habitable-structure performance and Route 487's substantial compatible-
infrastructure paralleling, lower cost, shorter length, and other cumulative advantages.

G. The PFD's "least bad option" characterization should not be converted into a
presumption favoring Route 894.

The PFD stated that the ALJs were "tasked with choosing the least bad option" and
recommended Route 894 "if any route must be chosen. "31 The J27 Landowners do not contend
that this wording constitutes legal error. But it is relevant to the weight the Commission should
give the recommendation.

A recommendation framed as the "least bad option" is not the same as a finding that Route
894 affirmatively best satisfies the statutory criteria. The Commission remains responsible for
independently balancing the record. That is particularly important where Staff independently
reached the opposite conclusion and recommended Route 487.

The Commission should therefore ask two straightforward questions. First, is the Central
Corridor justified when other reasonable corridors would reduce the line's proximity to the State
Parks? Second, if the Central Corridor is selected, do Route 894's park-proximity issues and
similar habitable structures outweigh Route 487's materially greater use of existing compatible
infrastructure, nearly four times the existing transmission-line paralleling, shorter length, lower
estimated transmission-line cost, favorable secondary metrics, and Staff's independent
recommendation? On this record, the J27 Landowners submit that the answer to both questions is
no.



IV. LIMITED REPLY REGARDING NOTICE AND PUBLIC INPUT

The J27 Landowners do not rely on the PFD's notice conclusions as an independent basis for
denial. The Commission's August 28,2026 order in Docket No. 59315 held that Rule
22.52(a)(4) requires at least one public meeting before filing but does not require an additional
meeting merely because route links are later added or the study area is expanded.33




                                                  10
 Applicants nevertheless use that decision to argue, in substance, that the post-meeting route
changes should have no significance beyond establishing compliance with the rule. The J27
Landowners respectfully disagree with that broader proposition. Compliance with Rule
22.52(a)(4) does not mean that the history of the route-development process becomes irrelevant
to the Commission's evaluation of community values, route development, or the weight to be
assigned to later-added corridors.

The PFD found that approximately 400 miles of route links were added after the June 2025
public meetings, bringing approximately 1,400 additional landowners into the filed routing
universe.34 Those facts may not establish a notice violation after Docket No. 59315, but they
remain relevant to understanding which portions of the final routing universe were available for
landowner input at the public meetings and which were developed later.

That distinction is particularly relevant to the Commission's understanding of the final routing
universe. The record shows that substantial portions of the filed routing universe were added or
modified after the public meetings. The Commission need not treat those changes as a notice
violation to recognize the route-development history as factual context when evaluating
community values, the development of alternatives, and the relative merits of the final routes.


V. REQUESTED DISPOSITION

The J27 Landowners respectfully request that the Commission reject the Exceptions that seek to
overturn the PFD's recommendation of denial and adopt the PFD's conclusion that Applicants
failed to establish the need for Import Path 2.

If the Commission nevertheless determines that the Project should proceed, the J27 Landowners
request that the Commission first consider whether a route outside the Central Corridor
provides a better overall balance of the statutory criteria and better protects Colorado Bend State
Park and Post Oak Ridge State Park. Route CCG is one record-supported example; Routes 296,
392, and 410 are additional examples raised in the Exceptions and record.

If the Commission nevertheless selects the Central Corridor, the J27 Landowners request
selection of Route 487 rather than Route 894. Route 894's mixed performance on park proximity
and similar habitable-structure count are minor advantages. They do not eliminate the Central
Corridor's broader park and viewshed impacts and do not outweigh Route 487's materially
greater use of existing compatible infrastructure, nearly four times the existing transmission-
line paralleling, shorter length, lower estimated transmission-line cost, favorable secondary
metrics, and Staff's independent recommendation.


VI. PROPOSED FINDINGS AND CONCLUSIONS

The J27 Landowners do not request a wholesale rewrite of the PFD. If the Commission adopts
the PFD's denial recommendation, the existing need findings and conclusions should be retained,

 subject to the Commission's August 28,2026 ruling in Docket No. 59315 concerning Rule
22.52(a)(4).

If the Commission reaches routing, the final order should expressly identify the relative weight
assigned to: (1) the State Park and viewshed evidence; (2) Route 487's 49.64 percent compatible-
ROW paralleling compared with Route 894's 43.92 percent; (3) Route 487's 22.05 miles of
existing transmission-line paralleling compared with 5.66 miles; (4) the $16.1 million
transmission-line cost difference and 1.7-mile length difference; (5) the 96-versus-85 broad
habitable-structure comparison and the narrower 85-versus-80 single-family comparison; and (6)
Staff's independent recommendation of Route 487.36


VII. CONCLUSION

For the reasons stated above, the J27 Landowners respectfully request that the Commission deny
the Applications because Applicants failed to establish that Import Path 2 is necessary for the
service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the public.

Alternatively, if the Commission approves the Project, it should first consider a non-Central-
Corridor alternative that better protects Colorado Bend State Park and Post Oak Ridge State
Park. If the Commission nevertheless selects the Central Corridor, it should select Route 487
rather than Route 894.
